title: 5 Simple Hacks That Will Cut Your Planning Time In Half ime-in-half/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin offers five practical strategies for dramatically reducing lesson planning time, framed around the idea that strong classroom management is itself the foundation that makes efficient planning possible. His hacks include becoming a classroom management expert so lessons can be designed freely without fear of poor execution; arriving early to capitalize on the mental clarity of a quiet morning; planning first thing, before checking email or engaging colleagues, to avoid early distractions; focusing on one task at a time rather than multitasking with classroom setup chores; and deliberately giving yourself less time to plan, since a tighter deadline sharpens focus and speeds decision-making. He closes by connecting these habits to a broader picture of teacher well-being, arguing that most teachers are overwhelmed and under-rested, and that reclaiming planning time through these hacks reduces stress and restores the capacity to be an inspiring, effective teacher.
points: Strong classroom management itself saves planning time by removing the fear that a lesson won't go well.
Arriving early and planning in the quiet morning hours produces clearer, more efficient thinking than planning after school.
Planning first thing, before checking email or engaging with colleagues, avoids early distractions that eat into time.
Focusing on one task at a time, rather than multitasking classroom chores, produces faster and higher-quality planning.
Deliberately shortening your planning window sharpens focus and speeds up decision-making, contrary to intuition.
quotes: Nothing saves more time than good, solid classroom management.

You’ll accomplish far more in the quiet of the morning than you ever will after school when distractions are great, energy stores are low, and the images of the day are still running through your head.
Dedicate your first block of time each morning to planning for the day or the week ahead. Shut your door, take a deep breath, and get down to it.
Teachers who try to multitask (studies show it isn’t really possible), tend to be absentminded, stressed-out , and disorganized.

Limiting your time—as long as it’s focused time—has an almost supernatural effect of speeding up your thinking. It immediately puts you into a flow state, where ideas are clear, solutions are apparent, and the path forward is obvious.
You’ll have more time to breathe and think and be the teacher your students so desperately need. The one you were meant to be.
